triage.name: Period Pain
triage.reason: Dysmenorrhea is a common, interview-reachable diagnosis with a clear presentation and important secondary causes (endometriosis, fibroids) to consider.

demographics: Primary dysmenorrhea usually begins within 6–12 months of menarche, once ovulatory cycles are established
Pain tends to lessen with increasing age and after childbirth
Secondary dysmenorrhea is more likely when pain begins after age 25 or worsens over time
family_history: Painful periods in a mother or sister
social_history: Pain that interferes with school, work, or daily activities

chief_complaints.text: I get bad cramps in my lower belly every month
The pain is so bad I miss school or work

hpi.onset: Cramping starts a day or two before or on the first day of bleeding; in primary dysmenorrhea it began within the first year or two after periods started
hpi.duration: Typically 1–3 days per cycle, sometimes longer
hpi.progression: Pain is worst on the first day or two of the period and eases over the next few days; it recurs in a similar pattern each cycle rather than steadily worsening
hpi.location: Lower abdomen, often midline or slightly to one side
hpi.radiation: May spread to the lower back, inner thighs, or upper legs
hpi.quality: Cramping, throbbing, or aching; comes in waves
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; often 5–8/10 at its worst and enough to interfere with usual activities
hpi.timing: Cyclical, tied to the menstrual period; not present between periods
aggravating: The first day or two of bleeding
relieving: Heating pad or hot bath on the lower abdomen
Ibuprofen or naproxen started at the first sign of cramps
pertinent_negatives: Fever or chills with the period
Missed period or positive pregnancy test
Pain that has been getting steadily worse over months
Pain that continues after the period ends

positives.text: Heavy or prolonged bleeding with periods
Irritability or low mood before the period

atypical.how_it_differs: Adolescents may describe the pain vaguely as a stomachache and miss school rather than report cramps; primary dysmenorrhea usually starts within 6–12 months of menarche.
New or worsening severe period pain after age 25 suggests secondary dysmenorrhea from endometriosis, fibroids, or adenomyosis rather than primary dysmenorrhea.
Obesity is associated with heavier bleeding and more painful periods, and can make pelvic examination and imaging less straightforward.

general.mild: Comfortable between cramps; mild discomfort during the visit, no distress
general.moderate: Winces or shifts position with cramps; appears uncomfortable but not ill
general.severe: Visibly uncomfortable, curls up or holds the lower abdomen, may look pale or diaphoretic
general.critical: Ill-appearing, pale, diaphoretic, or in acute distress — suggests a secondary cause such as a ruptured cyst, ectopic pregnancy, or pelvic infection

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, starting away from the area of pain
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen without guarding or rebound
Mild suprapubic tenderness without peritoneal signs

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to cough, or gently percuss the abdomen
findings.finding: No rebound or guarding; no pain with jarring

findings.maneuver: Auscultate bowel sounds in all four quadrants

findings.finding: Normal external genitalia without lesions, ulcers, or abnormal discharge

findings.maneuver: Perform a bimanual pelvic exam and move the cervix side to side
Palpate the uterus and adnexa bimanually
findings.finding: Normal-sized, mobile, non-tender uterus; no adnexal masses or tenderness
Unilateral or bilateral adnexal mass or fullness

findings.maneuver: Perform a rectal exam when a pelvic mass or gastrointestinal source is suspected
findings.finding: No mass, tenderness, or blood on the glove

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin for rash, petechiae, or jaundice

labs.caveat: Negative. Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy in anyone of reproductive age with pelvic pain before imaging or treatment.
Low only when periods are heavy enough to cause iron deficiency; supports a secondary cause such as fibroids rather than primary dysmenorrhea.
Low ferritin points to iron deficiency from heavy menstrual bleeding.
Usually normal in primary dysmenorrhea; a marked rise suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or another inflammatory process.
Normal in primary dysmenorrhea; elevated in pelvic infection or advanced endometriosis.
Mild sterile pyuria can occur from contamination or adjacent inflammation; a positive nitrite or heavy leukocyte esterase with symptoms points to urinary infection instead.
Positive nitrite argues against dysmenorrhea and toward a urinary tract infection.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging in adults; best resolution for the uterus and adnexa

findings.text: Normal uterus and ovaries with no structural abnormality (primary dysmenorrhea)
Enlarged, heterogeneous, or globular uterus with myometrial cysts or asymmetric wall thickening (adenomyosis)
Endometrioma — a homogeneous low-level internal echo ovarian cyst
Thickened or fluid-filled fallopian tube or tubo-ovarian complex (pelvic inflammatory disease)

imaging.preferred_when: Patients who have not been sexually active, or when transvaginal imaging is declined or not possible

findings.text: Large fibroids or adnexal masses may be seen; smaller lesions are often missed
Distended bladder required as an acoustic window

imaging.preferred_when: When ultrasound is nondiagnostic and adenomyosis or deep endometriosis is suspected

findings.text: Junctional zone thickening and myometrial cysts (adenomyosis)
Deep infiltrating endometriosis involving the uterosacral ligaments, rectum, or bladder
Fibroids characterized by location and size

imaging.preferred_when: When endometriosis is strongly suspected and imaging is unrevealing, or when symptoms persist despite treatment

findings.text: Endometrial implants on the peritoneum, ovaries, or pelvic sidewalls

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Usually normal or nonspecific in dysmenorrhea; not a first-line test
May incidentally show fibroids, adnexal masses, or free fluid

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy in anyone of reproductive age with pelvic pain
Checks for anemia from heavy menstrual bleeding and for leukocytosis suggesting infection
Screens for urinary tract infection or stone, a common mimic of pelvic pain
First-line imaging to look for fibroids, adenomyosis, endometriomas, or other structural causes
initial.only_if: pain is severe, new after age 25, worsening, or not responding to NSAIDs

initial.why: Alternative when transvaginal imaging is not possible
initial.only_if: patient has not been sexually active or declines transvaginal study

confirmatory.why: Definitive for endometriosis or adhesions when imaging is unrevealing and symptoms persist
confirmatory.only_if: secondary dysmenorrhea is strongly suspected and imaging is nondiagnostic

supporting.why: Confirms iron deficiency from heavy bleeding
supporting.only_if: heavy menstrual bleeding or anemia is present

supporting.why: Supports pelvic inflammatory disease when infection is suspected
supporting.only_if: fever, purulent discharge, or cervical motion tenderness is present

supporting.why: Adds to the inflammatory picture when infection or advanced endometriosis is suspected
supporting.only_if: infection or deep endometriosis is suspected

supporting.why: Characterizes adenomyosis or deep endometriosis when ultrasound is inconclusive
supporting.only_if: ultrasound is nondiagnostic and adenomyosis or deep endometriosis is suspected

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not a first-line test for dysmenorrhea; exposes the patient to radiation without adding diagnostic value
Invasive; not needed for typical primary dysmenorrhea that responds to NSAIDs
No role in cyclical pelvic pain
Not needed unless pain is epigastric or radiates to the back
Rarely changes management of pelvic pain

decision_points: Pregnancy test before any imaging or treatment in anyone who could be pregnant
Pelvic exam and ultrasound when pain is new after age 25, worsening, or not responding to NSAIDs
Fever, purulent discharge, or cervical motion tenderness prompts testing for pelvic inflammatory disease
Sudden severe one-sided pain with a positive or unknown pregnancy status is an emergency — evaluate for ectopic pregnancy

differential.name: Endometriosis
differential.why_considered: Cyclical pelvic pain that is severe, worsens over time, or begins later in life is often caused by endometriosis rather than primary dysmenorrhea.
differential.trigger: Pain that is progressively worse each cycle, deep pain with intercourse, or pain that continues after the period ends

history: Pain that has been getting steadily worse over months to years
Deep pain with intercourse
Pain with bowel movements or urination during the period
Pain that begins before the period and continues after it ends
Infertility or difficulty conceiving
exam: Tenderness or nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments or posterior fornix
labs: CA-125 may be elevated but is not diagnostic
imaging: Endometrioma — a homogeneous low-level internal echo ovarian cyst on ultrasound
Deep infiltrating implants involving the uterosacral ligaments, rectum, or bladder on MRI
Normal-appearing pelvis on imaging does not exclude the diagnosis

differential.name: Uterine fibroids
differential.why_considered: Fibroids are a common cause of secondary dysmenorrhea, especially with heavy or prolonged bleeding.

history: Heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding
Pelvic pressure, fullness, or bloating
Urinary frequency from mass effect
Pain that is more constant or pressure-like than purely cramping
labs: Anemia or low ferritin from chronic heavy bleeding
imaging: Well-circumscribed hypoechoic myometrial masses on ultrasound
Fibroids characterized by location and size on MRI

differential.name: Adenomyosis
differential.why_considered: Adenomyosis causes heavy, painful periods and an enlarged, tender uterus, and is easily mistaken for primary dysmenorrhea.

history: Heavy menstrual bleeding with progressively worsening cramps
Pain that persists beyond the period
Onset later in reproductive life, often after age 30
History of uterine surgery or childbirth
exam: Diffusely enlarged, boggy, and tender uterus
imaging: Enlarged, heterogeneous, or globular uterus with myometrial cysts or asymmetric wall thickening on ultrasound
Junctional zone thickening and myometrial cysts on MRI

differential.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain in a sexually active patient can be infectious rather than menstrual, and delaying treatment risks infertility.
differential.trigger: Fever, purulent vaginal discharge, or cervical motion tenderness with pelvic pain

history: Vaginal discharge, often purulent or foul-smelling
New or multiple sexual partners
Fever and chills
Pain that is not strictly cyclical and may be worse with movement
labs: Positive nucleic acid testing for gonorrhea or chlamydia
imaging: Thickened or fluid-filled fallopian tube or tubo-ovarian complex on ultrasound

differential.name: Ovarian cyst rupture or torsion
differential.why_considered: Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain can be a gynecologic emergency rather than ordinary period cramps.
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset of severe unilateral pelvic pain, especially with vomiting at the start

history: Sudden onset of severe one-sided pain
Vomiting at the onset of pain
Known ovarian cyst
Pain not relieved by NSAIDs or heat
exam: Peritoneal signs if rupture has occurred
imaging: Enlarged ovary with reduced Doppler flow on ultrasound (torsion)

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Any reproductive-age patient with pelvic pain could have an ectopic pregnancy, which is life-threatening if missed.
differential.trigger: Any patient who could be pregnant with pelvic pain

history: Missed period
Vaginal bleeding or spotting
Unilateral pelvic pain
Shoulder pain or syncope suggesting intra-abdominal bleeding
imaging: No intrauterine pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound

differential.name: Premenstrual syndrome
differential.why_considered: PMS causes cyclical symptoms that patients may describe as period pain, but the timing and nature of symptoms differ.

history: Symptoms begin one to two weeks before the period and resolve with bleeding
Bloating, breast tenderness, irritability, and fatigue predominate
Pain is not the primary complaint

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Lower abdominal pain and discomfort can be urinary rather than menstrual, especially if symptoms are not strictly cyclical.

history: Dysuria, urgency, and frequency
Suprapubic discomfort not tied to the menstrual cycle
No cyclical pattern
labs: Positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite on urinalysis

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: IBS can cause cramping lower abdominal pain and changes in bowel habits that overlap with menstrual cramps.

history: Pain related to bowel movements or changes in stool form
Bloating and alternating constipation and diarrhea
Symptoms not strictly limited to the menstrual period
exam: Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs
labs: Normal CBC, CRP, and celiac serology

severity.mild: Cramping that is noticeable but does not limit activities; responds to heat or a single dose of an NSAID; no missed school or work
severity.moderate: Cramping that interferes with daily activities, requires scheduled NSAIDs, and may cause missed school or work; associated nausea, headache, or back pain
severity.severe: Incapacitating pain despite NSAIDs, with vomiting, diarrhea, or syncope; unable to function for one or more days each cycle; raises concern for secondary dysmenorrhea
severity.critical: Not applicable — primary dysmenorrhea itself is not life-threatening; critical presentations suggest a different diagnosis such as ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, or pelvic infection

red_flags.finding: Fever or chills with pelvic pain
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or another infection; needs prompt evaluation and antibiotics
Suggests ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst, or ectopic pregnancy; a surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Positive or unknown pregnancy test with pelvic pain
Pain or bleeding between periods, or pain that continues after the period ends
red_flags.meaning: Suggests secondary dysmenorrhea such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, or fibroids
Suggests secondary rather than primary dysmenorrhea; warrants pelvic exam and imaging

red_flags.finding: Pain that is progressively worsening over months
red_flags.meaning: Suggests an underlying structural or inflammatory cause
Suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or another genital infection

red_flags.finding: Syncope or shoulder pain with pelvic pain
red_flags.meaning: Suggests intra-abdominal bleeding, as in a ruptured ectopic pregnancy

complications.name: Iron deficiency anemia from heavy menstrual bleeding
Missed school or work and reduced quality of life
clues: Anxiety or low mood related to cycles

special_populations.differences: Adolescents may describe the pain vaguely as a stomachache and miss school rather than report cramps; primary dysmenorrhea usually starts within 6–12 months of menarche once ovulatory cycles are established.
New or worsening severe period pain after age 25 suggests secondary dysmenorrhea from endometriosis, fibroids, or adenomyosis rather than primary dysmenorrhea.
Dysmenorrhea does not occur during pregnancy; pelvic pain in pregnancy must be evaluated for ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, or other obstetric causes.
Obesity is associated with heavier bleeding and more painful periods, and can make pelvic examination and imaging less straightforward.

key_questions.question: When did the pain start in relation to your period, and how long does it last?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain starting a day or two before or on the first day of bleeding and lasting 1–3 days, recurring each cycle

key_questions.question: Where is the pain, and does it spread anywhere?
key_questions.looking_for: Lower abdominal midline cramping that may radiate to the lower back or inner thighs

key_questions.question: What does the pain feel like, and how bad is it on a 0–10 scale?
key_questions.looking_for: Cramping, throbbing, or aching pain that comes in waves, often 5–8/10 at its worst

key_questions.question: What makes the pain better or worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse on the first day or two of bleeding and with activity; better with heat, NSAIDs, rest, or hormonal birth control

key_questions.question: Does the pain interfere with school, work, or your usual activities?
key_questions.looking_for: Missed school or work and reduced daily functioning during the period

key_questions.question: How old were you when your periods started, and when did the painful periods begin?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain beginning within 6–12 months of menarche suggests primary dysmenorrhea; new pain after age 25 suggests a secondary cause

key_questions.question: Has the pain been getting worse over time, or is it about the same each cycle?
key_questions.looking_for: Stable cyclical pain suggests primary dysmenorrhea; steadily worsening pain suggests endometriosis, adenomyosis, or fibroids

key_questions.question: Do you have pain or bleeding between periods, or pain that continues after your period ends?
key_questions.looking_for: Present symptoms suggest secondary dysmenorrhea rather than primary

key_questions.question: Do you have pain with intercourse or with bowel movements during your period?
key_questions.looking_for: Deep dyspareunia or dyschezia suggests endometriosis

key_questions.question: How heavy are your periods, and how long do they last?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy or prolonged bleeding suggests fibroids, adenomyosis, or iron deficiency anemia

key_questions.question: Do you have nausea, diarrhea, headache, or back pain with your periods?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, and lower back pain commonly accompany dysmenorrhea

key_questions.question: Do you have a fever, chills, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge with the pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Present symptoms suggest pelvic inflammatory disease or another infection

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Missed period or possible pregnancy raises concern for ectopic pregnancy

key_questions.question: Have you ever had sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt severe unilateral pain suggests ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst, or ectopic pregnancy

key_questions.question: What have you tried for the pain, and does it help?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs started at the first sign of cramps, heat, rest, exercise, or hormonal birth control that relieves symptoms

key_questions.question: Have you been pregnant or given birth before?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain often lessens after childbirth; nulliparity is a weak risk factor

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have painful periods or endometriosis?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of painful periods or endometriosis in a first-degree relative

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol, or use any drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Smoking is a weak risk factor; alcohol and tobacco may worsen symptoms

key_questions.question: Are you sexually active, and do you use contraception?
key_questions.looking_for: Sexual history guides pregnancy testing, pelvic exam, and testing for sexually transmitted infections

key_questions.question: Have you had any abdominal or pelvic surgery?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior uterine surgery or childbirth is associated with adenomyosis

reasoning_points: Cyclical lower abdominal cramping that starts a day or two before or on the first day of bleeding and lasts 1–3 days
Pain began within 6–12 months of menarche and has a stable, recurring pattern rather than worsening over time
Associated nausea, diarrhea, headache, and lower back pain are common
Pain is relieved by heat, NSAIDs started at the first sign of cramps, rest, or hormonal birth control
No pain or bleeding between periods, no dyspareunia, no fever or purulent discharge, and no pain after the period ends
Pelvic examination is normal with no cervical motion tenderness, adnexal mass, or enlarged tender uterus
Pregnancy is excluded in anyone of reproductive age with pelvic pain
Imaging is normal when obtained, supporting primary rather than secondary dysmenorrhea

Classic cyclical cramping on the first day or two of the period
Relieved by ibuprofen or a heating pad
medium: Woman of reproductive age with heavy bleeding and anemia
Pain that interferes with school or work despite NSAIDs
Nausea, diarrhea, and headache prominent with the cramps
Pelvic ultrasound needed to exclude fibroids or adenomyosis
hard: New severe cramps after age 25 suggesting secondary dysmenorrhea
Pain that is progressively worsening over months
Deep dyspareunia or dyschezia suggesting endometriosis
Adolescent who describes the pain vaguely as a stomachache and misses school
Pain that continues after the period ends or occurs between periods
